issues.quote: One little man measured the Saturnian. He was right!
issues.problem: The little man's measurement is never stated, so the reader cannot tell what he was 'right' about. 'He' could also mean the Saturnian. A1 readers will stop here.
issues.fix: One little man measured the Saturnian. "You are one mile tall," he said. He was right!

notes: "He flew from star to star. At last, he came to Saturn." Saturn is a planet, not a star. 'from world to world' would be more accurate, but the sentence reads naturally as it is.
"Then a tiny man in a hat spoke." The other levels say a square cap. A 'hat' is an acceptable simplification.
"An important old official": the original calls the mufti ignorant and petty, but not old. The word 'old' is harmless.
"This planet has a very bad shape" is slightly stiff. 'This planet is a very ugly shape' would read more naturally.
"where they measured the shape of the Earth": 'had gone to measure' would be clearer, but the past simple is acceptable at B1.
"Micromegas had to leave the court": 'court' appears here without being introduced. 'his country's court' would help.
"To prove it, one of the scientists pointed his instruments..." 'It' (that they could think) is slightly loose. 'To show what they could do' would be clearer.

"he had worked out more of the laws of geometry by himself than most scholars learn in a lifetime" exaggerates the original, where he discovered about fifty of Euclid's propositions on his own (more than Pascal). This is acceptable condensing.
"aimed his instruments at the Saturnian and announced that the Saturnian was about a mile tall" repeats 'the Saturnian'. Use 'announced that he stood about a mile tall'.

summary: This retelling follows Voltaire's Micromegas closely at every level: the banned insect book, the 220-year trial, the senses and lifespans, Mars's moons, the 5 July 1737 landing, the diamond microscopes, the fingernail speaking tube, the measurement, the heap-of-mud war, the Lockean who admits ignorance, the square-capped Thomist and the blank book. The war is only mentioned, never shown, so it suits the 4+ rating. The only failure is at A1, where 'He was right!' follows a measurement whose result is never given.
